To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
overreporting on the MMPI is a problem among Vietnam veterans, especially in-country combat veterans.

a high number (20.6%) of subjects randomly responded on the MMPI, that in-country veterans reported significantly more symptoms on the MMPI than Vietnam-era veterans, and that overreporters reported significantly more symptoms than acceptable subjects.

a high number (nearly 1/3) of subjects randomly responded, in-country veterans met overreporting criteria more than did the Vietnam-era group, and that MANOVAs showed differences among groups in the MMPI basic scales, the Harris-Lingoes subscales, the MMPI Test-Retest scale, and the S-O scale.

the problem area of overreporting of MMPI responses by Vietnam veterans.
overreporting on the MMPI.
the overreporting of symptoms by Vietnam veterans.

the overreporting of symptoms by Vietnam veterans is a real phenomenon.
overreporting is a problem among in-country Vietnam veterans, and the overreporting problem is not as prevalent in the Vietnam-era veterans.
the Vietnam combat veteran is not a reliable source of data on his or her mental status.

the Vietnam veteran who was in combat and who is overreporting on the MMPI is a different person than the Vietnam-era veteran.

there is a lot of variation in how people think about their experiences in Vietnam.
